strengths: Novel application of chaos theory (Lyapunov exponents, DFA) to discriminator design for speech bandwidth extension
Comprehensive ablation studies (Tables 1-2) systematically evaluating component contributions
Achieves parameter efficiency (33.5M parameters) with competitive or superior performance versus larger baselines
Multiple complementary objective evaluation metrics (6 metrics across fidelity, intelligibility, and perceptual quality)
Detailed experimental reporting including hyperparameters, dataset specifications, and hardware configuration
weaknesses: CRITICAL: Fundamental venue mismatch for ACL 2026—this is signal processing research without language processing components; better suited for ICASSP/Interspeech

Manuscript appears incomplete: Figures 2-3 labeled 'Dummy' without actual captions; subjective evaluation claimed in abstract but zero results shown; abstract lists MS-RD and MR-PPD not described anywhere in paper

Severely limited experimental validation: single dataset (VCTK, clean English only); no cross-dataset testing, noisy speech evaluation, or multilingual validation despite being essential for robustness claims

Weak theoretical justification: core hypothesis that discriminators capturing Lyapunov exponents improve reconstruction lacks rigorous mechanistic explanation; no empirical validation that these properties are actually captured

Marginal empirical improvements: NISQA-MOS gains over MS-BWE often <0.1 (4.24 vs 4.26); performance actually degrades for 2-48 kHz range (NISQA-MOS 3.9987) with no analysis; SI-SDR/SI-SNR similar or worse than baselines
Incomplete baseline comparisons: Table 3 has numerous 'NA' values; NU-Wave/EBEN/AERO results missing; cannot fairly assess claimed state-of-the-art status
Subjective evaluation claims unverifiable: abstract mentions 'five human judges' but paper provides no methodology, results, MOS scores, or inter-rater reliability

Missing critical implementation details: delay embedding parameters (d, τ) for MRLD unspecified; MSDFA tile size S undefined; adversarial loss weighting scheme never described; reproducibility severely compromised
Unclear contribution boundaries: paper conflates novel components (MRLD, MSDFA) with prior work (MRAD, MRPD acknowledged from Lu et al. 2024b); actual novelty contribution difficult to isolate
Presentation quality issues: dummy figures indicating incomplete work; grammatical errors; unexplained components (Schrodinger Bridge); Figure 1 caption uninformative; suggests rushed submission

strengths: Comprehensive experimental methodology with multiple evaluation metrics (LSD, STOI, PESQ, SI-SDR, SI-SNR, NISQA-MOS)
Thorough ablation studies examining individual components (Tables 1-2)
Achieves parameter efficiency (33.5M parameters vs. 72M for AP-BWE) through architectural optimization
Well-organized experimental setup with clear hyperparameter specification
weaknesses: CRITICAL SCOPE ISSUE: Paper is fundamentally a signal processing contribution with no computational linguistics content - should not be submitted to ACL
Weak theoretical justification: connection between chaos-theoretic measures and audio quality improvement is asserted but not rigorously validated
Non-standard application of chaos theory: computing Lyapunov exponents on 64-512 sample windows violates standard requirements for LE estimation (requires much longer time series)

Marginal improvements over baselines: MRLD+MSDFA vs. MPD achieves only 0.11 NISQA-MOS improvement (4.29 vs 4.18); parameter reduction primarily from depthwise separable convolution, not discriminators
Missing subjective evaluation: paper claims 'subjective based tests comprise of five human judges' but provides no MOS table or results
Incomplete contribution: abstract claims seven discriminators but only two (MRLD, MSDFA) are clearly described; MS-RD and MR-PPD are barely mentioned
Limited experimental scope: single clean-speech dataset (VCTK), no cross-dataset generalization, no noisy conditions, no multilingual evaluation

Poor presentation quality: grammatical errors ('genetor', 'benchmakr'), confusing Figure 1, algorithms missing critical parameter specifications (d, τ for delay-embedding; S for MSDFA tiling), opening sentence references non-existent prior discussion
Unclear attribution of gains: difficult to isolate improvements from chaos-inspired discriminators vs. architectural choices (ConformerNeXt, Lattice-Net, DSC)
Missing implementation details: depth-wise separable convolution parameters not fully specified; no code availability; reproducibility of complex chaos-theoretic components unclear

strengths: Solid empirical contribution with demonstrated parameter efficiency (40× reduction in discriminators vs. MPD while maintaining better perceptual quality); well-motivated application of chaos theory concepts (Lyapunov exponents, detrended fluctuation analysis) to capture nonlinear speech dynamics; comprehensive ablation studies (Tables 1-2) systematically validate each architectural component; extensive evaluation across multiple frequency ranges and six complementary objective metrics; thorough comparison showing practical advantages for edge deployment with 0.5× parameters vs. AP-BWE

Clear architectural presentation of the dual-stream generator with Lattice block interaction and ConformerNeXt blocks; well-documented experimental setup with detailed hyperparameters, dataset information, and hardware configuration supporting reproducibility; consistent improvements across perceptual quality metrics (NISQA-MOS, LSD, PESQ) demonstrating effectiveness of the proposed discriminator framework
weaknesses: Weak theoretical justification for chaos-based discriminators: the claim that speech exhibits 'deterministic chaos' lacks rigorous support; primary citation (Little et al., 2007) concerns voice disorders, not normal speech; the connection between matching Lyapunov spectra and improved audio quality is assumed rather than mechanistically demonstrated; unclear how computing LE on local windows actually captures meaningful chaotic dynamics

Critical gap in subjective evaluation: abstract promises 'subjective based tests comprises of five human judges' but Section 4 provides no methodology, sample size, inter-rater reliability, or results; this is a major omission for a paper claiming perceptual quality improvements

Technical clarity issues: Algorithm 1 (MRLD) has vague notation and undefined parameters (embedding dimension d, delay τ); Algorithm 2 (MSDFA) unclear on how 1D fluctuation signal tiles into S×S map; phase recovery via separate FFNNs (Eq. 2) lacks justification; hyperparameter choices (window sizes, scales) not justified or subjected to sensitivity analysis

Significant discrepancies in claims: abstract mentions 'four new discriminators' and 'seven discriminators' but actual method uses only four (MRLD, MSDFA, MRAD, MRPD); MS-RD and MR-PPD mentioned in abstract are absent from methodology; generator architecture novelty is limited—ConformerNeXt is merely replacing Conformer's conv with ConvNeXt (incremental), Lattice Net and dual-stream are existing techniques

Narrow experimental scope severely limiting generalizability claims: evaluation on single dataset (VCTK, English only, noise-free); no testing on multilingual data or noisy conditions despite listing as 'limitations'; incomplete baseline comparisons with missing results in Table 3 for NU-Wave, EBEN, AERO; marginal improvements on key metrics (SI-SDR/SI-SNR similar to AP-BWE, not better); no statistical significance testing

Writing quality issues: typo in abstract ('genetor' for 'generator'), grammatical errors ('leverage' vs 'leverages'), placeholder captions ('Dummy' for Figures 2-3) indicating incomplete preparation; incomplete technical justification (why Lattice Net needed? why complex-valued operations? why log-magnitude residuals?)

strengths: Novel application of chaos theory (Lyapunov exponents, detrended fluctuation analysis) to speech bandwidth extension with clear scientific motivation
Significant parameter efficiency achieving 0.5x fewer parameters than AP-BWE (33.5M vs 72M) with better perceptual quality on NISQA-MOS, PESQ, and STOI metrics

Comprehensive experimental evaluation including 6 objective metrics, subjective MOS/pairwise preference tests, computational complexity analysis (MACs, FLOPs, RTF), and detailed ablation studies justifying design choices
Excellent reproducibility with extensive hyperparameter tables, dataset preprocessing details, architecture specifications, and inference workflows in appendices
Thorough technical presentation with dual-stream processing, Lattice-based stream interaction, and well-engineered generator architecture demonstrating solid engineering
weaknesses: Critically limited evaluation scope: tested only on VCTK (English, read speech) in noise-free settings with no cross-dataset, cross-lingual, or robustness evaluation—severely undermines generalizability claims and practical applicability

Unclear mechanism for chaos-based improvements: paper asserts Lyapunov exponents and DFA capture relevant features but provides no rigorous justification; ablation shows only +0.15 NISQA-MOS from adding MSDFA, suggesting incremental gains; missing analysis of what chaos discriminators actually learn differently

Missing critical technical details: delay-embedding parameters (d, τ) unspecified in Algorithm 1; unclear how Lyapunov exponents remain differentiable for backpropagation; DFA typically requires longer time series but used on 6-37ms windows; size S for tiling F(n) not specified

Limited novelty: applies classical techniques (Lyapunov exponents from 1968, DFA from 1994) to discriminators (incremental); ConformerNeXt is straightforward combination of Conformer and ConvNeXt; Lattice blocks from prior work; all loss functions are standard

Mixed performance on key metrics: SI-SDR and SI-SNR worsen compared to AP-BWE (13.24 vs 13.42 dB, 13.15 vs 13.35 dB); improvements primarily on NISQA-MOS (learned metric) and PESQ; modest 11% subjective preference with insufficient statistical validation

Weak subjective evaluation: only 10 participants (all Bangladeshi undergraduates, non-native English speakers), 30 samples per person, no confidence intervals or significance testing, 11% preference improvement over AP-BWE is marginal

Severe dataset limitations: VCTK contains read newspaper articles (not natural speech); limited to single language (English); no evaluation on noisy, reverberant, or realistic speech; only 110 speakers; no cross-speaker generalization analysis

Missing experimental rigor: no error bars or confidence intervals reported; no statistical significance testing between methods; no cross-validation; no analysis of failure cases; training time not compared with baselines; incomplete justification for loss weight selection (λ values appear arbitrary)

strengths: Novel application of chaos theory (Lyapunov exponents, DFA) to speech bandwidth extension with clear theoretical motivation provided in Appendix A.1
Comprehensive ablation studies (Tables 2-3) systematically evaluating discriminator and generator components with transparent parameter reporting
Efficient model design achieving 0.5x fewer parameters than AP-BWE baseline for practical deployment
Extensive multi-faceted evaluation including six objective metrics, subjective MOS/preference tests, and assessment across multiple frequency ranges
Detailed reproducibility documentation with extensive hyperparameter tables, preprocessing pipeline descriptions, and implementation details in appendices
weaknesses: Core claim that MRLD/MSDFA capture deterministic chaos is unvalidated: no evidence they extract chaotic features, no demonstration that chaos modeling is necessary for BWE, and no ablation comparing identical architecture with/without chaos-informed discriminators

Marginal and inconsistent improvements over AP-BWE: NISQA-MOS gains narrow from 0.38 to near-zero across frequency ranges, while SI-SDR and SI-SNR actually underperform the baseline without statistical significance testing

Unfair experimental comparison: CIS-BWE differs from AP-BWE in three confounded ways (chaos discriminators, ConformerNeXt, Lattice interactions); Table 2's MRLD+MSDFA (483.2k) vs MPD (22M) comparison lacks parameter-matched controls

Limited scope and generalization: evaluated only on English VCTK corpus with 102 training speakers, no cross-lingual/cross-domain testing, no noisy/reverberant conditions despite claims of broad applicability

Unvalidated algorithmic components: Algorithm 1 computes Lyapunov exponents on short waveform segments without specifying embedding dimension d or delay τ; Algorithm 2 tiles DFA curves into fixed S×S maps destroying multi-scale structure that makes DFA valuable

Lack of rigorous statistical analysis: only 10 non-native English speakers for subjective evaluation with no confidence intervals, p-values, or significance testing; 2% improvement over baseline falls within typical evaluation noise

Overclaimed novelty and incremental contribution: primarily combines existing techniques (Lyapunov exponents, DFA, standard GANs, existing architectures); ConformerNeXt is straightforward module replacement in Conformer
Unexplained loss function complexity: six loss terms with manually tuned weights across four discriminators without ablation studies on necessity or sensitivity of individual components

Architectural complexity without clear justification: four ConformerNeXt blocks plus Lattice blocks with learnable scalars, but Table 3 shows linear alternative achieves comparable performance (3.72 vs 4.03 NISQA-MOS gain)

Missing validation of core mechanism: no analysis of whether computed 'Lyapunov exponents' correlate with perceptual quality, no visualization of learned chaos features, no ablation separating chaos contribution from other architectural improvements

strengths: Novel application of chaos-informed discriminators (MRLD, MSDFA) to complex-valued GANs for audio reconstruction, with sound theoretical motivation linking speech's deterministic chaos to improved reconstruction quality

Comprehensive experimental evaluation with 8 metrics across 3 frequency ranges, extensive ablations (Tables 2-3), and detailed parameter/computational complexity analysis demonstrating parameter efficiency (0.5× parameters vs. AP-BWE, 40× discriminator reduction)
Well-motivated dual-stream architecture combining ConformerNeXt with learnable Lattice gating for controlled magnitude-phase stream interaction, supported by ablation studies
Excellent presentation and reproducibility support: detailed architecture diagrams, layer-wise parameter breakdowns, complete hyperparameter specifications, and extensive appendices (A.1-A.9)
Practical efficiency gains: achieves competitive performance with 2.18× fewer parameters (33.5M vs. 72M) and lower computational complexity (MACs, FLOPs)
weaknesses: Weak theoretical justification for chaos ↔ BWE connection: paper establishes speech contains chaos but fails to rigorously explain why capturing chaotic properties specifically improves high-frequency recovery, and SI-SDR/SI-SNR metrics are essentially identical to AP-BWE, undermining claims that chaos modeling is essential
Severely limited experimental scope: only VCTK (single language, clean read speech, single domain); no multilingual, noisy, or cross-domain evaluation; claims of generalization are not supported

Modest and inconsistent improvements: NISQA-MOS gain of +0.38 over AP-BWE is clinically marginal; only 2% pairwise preference improvement (n=10 participants, 30 samples per listener, no statistical significance testing reported); core reconstruction metrics (SI-SDR, SI-SNR) identical to baseline

Critical hyperparameters unexplained and unablated: loss weights (λ_mag=45, λ_pha=100, etc.) lack justification; no ablation on number of resolutions (why 5?) or specific DFA scales (100,200,300,500,600?); discriminator contribution imbalance not analyzed

No validation that chaos features are actually learned: missing visualizations of Lyapunov/DFA feature maps; no diagnostic confirming MRLD/MSDFA detect chaotic properties; no comparison of learned representations vs. alternative discriminators

Technical clarity gaps: Algorithm 1 doesn't specify critical delay-embedding parameters (dimension d, delay τ); Algorithm 2 'tiling' to S×S maps is poorly explained; ε term in line 5 of Algorithm 1 unexplained

Small-scale, methodologically weak subjective evaluation: only 10 homogeneous participants (Bangladeshi undergraduates), 30 samples/listener; no confidence intervals, significance tests, or effect sizes; results fragmented without proper statistical analysis

Missing diagnostic analyses: no ablation isolating chaos discriminators' contribution from architectural improvements; no failure case analysis; no investigation of which frequency bands benefit from chaos modeling; no cross-speaker or cross-phoneme analysis

Reproducibility concerns: no code availability statement; proprietary MATLAB interface for subjective evaluation; statistical analyses absent; some training details unclear (convergence criteria, early stopping, training stability with 6 loss terms)
Limited relevance to ACL: paper is primarily speech signal processing; motivation mentions TTS/ASR but neither is evaluated; indirect connection to computational linguistics
